02/09/2025  PURPOSE AND VISION
VC283
            This section sets out the purpose of this planning scheme, and the vision and strategic direction
            for Victoria and the municipality.

            ACKNOWLEDGEMENT OF COUNTRY

            The Victorian Government acknowledges Traditional Owners in Victoria as the custodians of
            Country. We acknowledge their extraordinary strength and resilience in the face of historical and
            ongoing social, economic and legal injustices, maintaining their connection to Country.

            We pay our respects to Elders past and present, whose knowledge and wisdom have ensured the
            continuation of spiritual and cultural practices. We also acknowledge the diversity of First Peoples’
            communities in Victoria.

            We acknowledge that the long-lasting, far-reaching and intergenerational consequences of
            colonisation and dispossession continue to exist today and continue to cause harm. Colonisation
            has left entrenched systemic and structural racism and suffering, including through the laws and
            policies of the Colony of Victoria, which speci昀椀cally excluded First Peoples and their laws, lores,
            customs, languages and cultures. The Victorian Government has a responsibility to transform its
            systems and service delivery so First Peoples have decision-making power over matters that directly
            affect them.

            To address this exclusion, the Victorian Government commits to ongoing engagement with
            Traditional Owners and First Peoples to restore and strengthen their rights in this planning scheme.

13/03/2026  CONTEXT
C271card
            The Shire is located on the south east fringe of Melbourne and is one of eight ‘interface councils’
            that form the perimeter of metropolitan Melbourne, providing a transition between urban and rural
            areas. The municipality has an area of approximately 1,280 square kilometres, comprising a variety
            of landforms and landscapes.

            The northern part of the Shire is set in the foothills of the Dandenong Ranges, and includes the
            Bunyip State Park and the Cardinia Reservoir. The red volcanic soils around Gembrook are
            historically signi昀椀cant for agriculture. The area is located within two water catchments being the
            Yarra Valley and Westernport catchments.

            The Koo Wee Rup swamp and Western Port form the signi昀椀cant features of the southern part of
            the Shire and includes high quality agricultural land of State signi昀椀cance. The land is generally
            昀氀at alluvial plains that have been substantially cleared of vegetation. The exception to this is the
            Heath Hill area, an area that is recognised as being of landscape signi昀椀cance by the National Trust.

            The population within the Cardinia growth area is expected to grow 79 per cent from the estimated
            current population of around 112,000 people (October 2019) to approximately 200,000 people in
            2041.

13/03/2026  VISION
C271card    The Shire’s vision for the municipality is:

                   Cardinia Shire will be developed in a planned manner to enable present and future
                   generations to live healthy and productive lives and to enjoy the richness of the diverse and
                   distinctive characteristics of the Shire.
            Planning will sustain the wellbeing of the community and the environment by seeking to balance
            the competing needs of the environment, economic development and the community and in
            particular by:
               Developing a strong economic base.
               Recognising and protecting the diverse and signi昀椀cant environmental and cultural heritage
               values in the municipality.
               Providing a cohesive and safe built environment for people to live, work and visit.

            Settlement
02.03-1
            Most of the Shire’s population is located within the urban areas of Beacons昀椀eld, Of昀椀cer and
13/03/2026  Pakenham. These areas, along with Cardinia Shire’s newest suburb currently referred to as
C271card    Pakenham East, are part of the Casey-Cardinia South-east Growth Corridor of metropolitan
            Melbourne. This corridor will accommodate most of the future residential and commercial growth.
            The remainder of the population is located within Cardinia’s townships and rural residential areas.

            Settlement is primarily focused in ten precincts within the Shire's urban areas, as well as the rural
            townships listed in Table 1. In the urban area there are two precincts in the ‘Urban Established
            Areas’, being Beacons昀椀eld and Pakenham identi昀椀ed in the plan at Clause 02.04-2, and eight
            precincts in the ‘Urban Growth Areas’ identi昀椀ed in the plan at Clause 02.04-3, which cover Of昀椀cer,
            Of昀椀cer South, Pakenham East and part of Pakenham South.

            Subdivision restructure has occurred in several areas in the municipality which were subdivided

            vegetated. The development of housing on these lots at the density of the original subdivision is

            1. Direct residential development to:

2. Protect land in the Urban Established Areas from development that limits the future orderly
   and ef昀椀cient development of the land for urban purposes.

3. Support Emerald and Koo Wee Rup as a focus for higher order commercial and community

5. Develop Gembrook township as a major tourism destination based on a heritage theme and the
   scenic qualities of the area.

6. Consolidate and activate Koo Wee Rup’s commercial and civic town centre.
7. Provide for the restructuring of inappropriate subdivisions.
8. Provide a distinct character and identity for urban areas through retention of existing vegetation,

   respect for topography, appropriate streetscaping and provision of adequate open space.

Western Port Green Wedge
The Western Port Green Wedge encompasses the southern rural areas of Cardinia Shire and the
City of Casey. It covers a land area of approximately 746 square kilometres across both
municipalities and will be a permanent edge to Melbourne’s southeast. Approximately 615 square
kilometres is located within Cardinia Shire.
A large proportion of Cardinia’s Western Port Green Wedge has some of the best agricultural soil
in Melbourne. Important natural resources exist within this green wedge, with existing sand
extraction industry in operation around Lang Lang and potential for future extractive industry to
occur in the north. It also has important biodiversity values, particularly the internationally
signi昀椀cant Ramsar wetlands and habitat for endangered species including the southern brown
bandicoot and the growling grass frog.
There are a number of rural townships and localities that provide opportunities for non-urban
township living as well as providing a focus for local provision of services, schools and employment.
This green wedge also has important recreation assets such as the Pakenham Racing Club’s
racecourse in Tynong and a potential future third airport.
Council’s strategic directions for the green wedge are to:
1. Protect and facilitate the sustainable use of agricultural land, particularly land with soil that is

   of a high quality within the Western Port Green Wedge.
2. Maintain and enhance the Western Port Green Wedge biodiversity, landscape and environmental

   values.
3. Protect green wedge land by preventing further encroachment of urban development into the

   Cardinia Western Port Green Wedge.
4. Allow limited growth of Cardinia Western Port Green Wedge settlements where it is supported

   by an adopted township strategy.
5. To give effect to Council’s vision for the Cardinia Western Port Green Wedge.

13/03/2026  Activity centres
C271card    Of昀椀cer and Pakenham are designated Major Activity Centres. Beacons昀椀eld, Lakeside Boulevard
            and Lakeside Square are designated as a large Neighbourhood Activity Centre within the urban
            growth boundary. Emerald in the north and Koo Wee Rup in the south of the municipality are
            larger township Neighbourhood Activity Centres and there are smaller Neighbourhood Activity
            Centres dispersed throughout the municipality.

            Council’s strategic directions for the activity centres are to:

            1. Encouraging development that reinforces the hierarchy of activity centres in the urban area.

            2. Ensure the orderly expansion of the Pakenham Major Activity Centre.

            Environmental and landscape values
            The diverse landscapes within the Shire are one of the municipality’s strongest attributes. Five
            areas within the Shire are recognised as signi昀椀cant landscapes by the National Trust. These are
            the Western Port Coast, Heath Hill, Cockatoo Creek, Puf昀椀ng Billy Corridor and Menzies Creek
            Valley.

            The Shire contains a diverse environment with a wide range of native 昀氀ora and fauna habitats and
            is known to contain State and Nationally signi昀椀cant rare and threatened species including the
            Southern Brown Bandicoot, Growling Grass Frog, Swamp Skink, Masked Owl, Helmeted
            Honeyeater, Powerful Owl, Dwarf Galaxias, Australian Grayling, Emerald Star Bush, Matted
            Flax-Lily and indigenous grasslands.

            Most of the Shire is contained in the Western Port water catchment, which contains a Ramsar
            wetland, with a small northern section of the Shire in the Yarra water catchment.

            There is pressure to develop land in locations of high scenic value.

            The decline and fragmentation of habitats resulting in the loss of biodiversity is a key issue. Over
            75 per cent of the native vegetation in the Shire has been cleared leaving those areas of remnant
            vegetation of particular signi昀椀cance and value in terms of maintaining biodiversity.

            Council’s strategic directions for environmental and landscape values are to:

            1. Protect environmentally signi昀椀cant areas including the northern hills and the Western Port
               coast.

            2. Protect the natural environment and character of rural townships including remnant vegetation
               in the hills townships.

            3. Protect the Koo Wee Rup swamp area that contains important groundwater reserves and
               horticultural soils in the Western Port basin.

            4. Maintain and re-establish wildlife corridors.

            5. Maintain biodiversity especially in areas of signi昀椀cance.

            6. Protect the environmental qualities that contribute to the rural character of Maryknoll.

            7. Minimise the fragmentation of land and removal of vegetation in areas of high landscape value.

            8. Protect the scenic corridor of the Puf昀椀ng Billy Tourist Railway from extensive native vegetation
               removal and development that is inconsistent with the landscape values of the existing corridor.

            9. Protect signi昀椀cant landscapes recognised by the National Trust including the Western Port
               Coast, Heath Hill, Cockatoo Creek and Menzies Creek Valley from development that is
               inconsistent with the landscape values and built form of the surrounds.

            10. Protect landscapes that are an important element in the development of tourism.

13/03/2026  Environmental risks and amenity
C271card
            Areas within the Shire, particularly north of the Princes Highway, are prone to bush昀椀res due to
02.03-4     the topography and vegetation. During the 1983 Ash Wednesday 昀椀res, there was a signi昀椀cant loss
            of life and property in the Upper Beacons昀椀eld and Cockatoo areas.
13/03/2026
C271card    Bush昀椀re risk is the product of several factors including fuel levels, slope, climatic conditions,
            population and the degree of preparation of individual property owners to cope with a 昀椀re. Other
            factors such as the accessibility of land to 昀椀re 昀椀ghting vehicles and the availability of water will
            affect the risk levels for individual properties.

            The municipality has wide areas that are liable to 昀氀ooding, including the Koo Wee Rup Flood
            Protection District. Climate change will increase the risk from bush昀椀res and 昀氀ooding.

            The Shire's other environmental risks include water catchment management, stormwater, salinity
            and soil erosion.

            Water catchments are an integrated environmental system, and any development or actions
            undertaken in one part of a catchment may have an effect on other parts of the catchment. [21.02.1
            KI 1] Stormwater quality in both urban and rural areas need to be managed to minimise the impact
            of development on the environment.

            There are areas within the municipality with a shallow groundwater table that increases the potential
            for salinity and its impacts on infrastructure and the environment.

            Soil erosion occurs on steep land where there are dispersible soils and in areas prone to landslips
            as a result of native vegetation removal.

            Council’s strategic directions for environmental risks are to:

            1. Minimise the potential risk to life, property and the environment from the effects of bush昀椀re
               and 昀氀ooding and inundation.

            2. Mitigate the detrimental impacts of development on the operation and health of waterway
               systems and on stormwater quality.

            3. Discourage development that will be at risk from salinity or soil erosion or that will potentially
               increase the risk or extent of impacts from salinity or soil erosion.

            Natural resource management

            Agriculture

            Agricultural production from the Port Phillip and Western Port Region is estimated at around 15
            per cent of Victoria's annual gross value of agricultural production, has the highest average gross
            production value per hectare of any catchment management region in Victoria and is around four
            times greater than the State average.

            The Koo Wee Rup Swamp area, with its peaty clay soil, is recognised for its high quality agricultural
            land of State signi昀椀cance. This area grows 90 per cent of Australia’s asparagus, of which 50 per
            cent is exported annually. There have been some inappropriate subdivisions of agricultural land
            in the Koo Wee Rup Flood Protection District.

            The high quality red volcanic soils of the Gembrook area have an important potato producing
            history. The area has been affected by dieldrin contamination (detected in 1987) and the Potato
            Cyst Nematode (detected in 1992) which resulted in restrictions on cattle grazing and potato
            production. Despite these restrictions, various forms of viable agriculture can be maintained.

            Given the importance of agricultural land to the economic viability of the area and the State,
            Council’s strategic directions for agriculture are to:

            1. Protect agricultural land, particularly areas of high quality soils, from the intrusion of urban
               uses, incompatible development and fragmentation that would lead to a reduction in agricultural

            Page 10 of 1548
02.03-5                                            CARDINIA PLANNING SCHEME

13/03/2026     viability, the erosion of the right of farmers to farm land, and ultimately the loss of land from
C271card       agricultural production.

            2. Provide for the establishment of intensive agricultural activities (e.g.: poultry farms and green
               houses) in a location and manner that minimises the impact on nearby residents and the
               environment

            3. Support the restructure of inappropriate subdivisions in agricultural areas, including the Koo
               Wee Rup Flood Protection District, to reduce the impact of old and inappropriate subdivisions
               on the agricultural viability.

            Extractive industries
            In the Shire, there are identi昀椀ed Extractive Industry Interest Areas (EIIA), which signi昀椀cantly
            overlap with areas of high environmental and landscape values.

            There are signi昀椀cant stone resources, being hard rock which is extracted primarily from the hills
            north of the Princes Highway.

            The Lang Lang to Grantville region contains signi昀椀cant sand resources which are expected to
            become a major source of sand for the Melbourne supply area over the next 10 to 20 years. The
            extraction of the sand resources will have signi昀椀cant economic, social and environmental effects
            on the area.

            There are potential amenity impacts from extractive industry operations including noise, dust,
            transport and blast vibration.

            Council’s strategic directions for extractive industries are to:

            1. Protect sand and stone resources and existing extractive industry operations from development
               that may impact on their viability.

            Built environment and heritage

            Urban design
            The long-term bene昀椀ts of good design are a more attractive, functional and sustainable built
            environment. Good design is based on the principle of being site responsive, designing to consider
            the character and constraints of a site and wider area.

            Conserving, reducing and effectively managing the resources we use are essential to achieving
            ecological sustainable development. The use of fossil fuels, particularly in electricity generation
            and transport has been the major source of greenhouse gas emissions resulting in climate change.
            Three key areas for reducing the impact on the environment within the municipality are air, water
            and general waste.

            Council’s strategic directions for heritage are to:

            1. Support building design that engages with the public realm and assists in increasing safety and
               the perception of safety for the community.

            2. Encourage the use of environmentally sustainable design and construction materials.

            3. Protect exotic vegetation if it is of heritage, cultural or economic value, or contributes to the
               character of an area.

            Heritage
            The Shire contains Aboriginal heritage sites and places of cultural signi昀椀cance, some of which
            have been identi昀椀ed and formally recorded but many which have not. Council seeks to ensure
            heritage sites and places are preserved for current and future generations.

            Page 11 of 1548
02.03-6                                            CARDINIA PLANNING SCHEME

13/03/2026  The rich and diverse cultural heritage of the Shire illustrates the historic use, development and
C271card    occupation of the land. This history is demonstrated by a wide range of heritage places that include
            buildings and structures, monuments, trees, landscapes and archaeological sites. These places give
02.03-7     Cardinia a sense of historic continuity as well as demonstrating the economic, social and political
            circumstances of the time.
13/03/2026
C271card    Council’s strategic directions for heritage are to:

            1. Identify and protect sites of signi昀椀cant Aboriginal heritage.

            2. Protect places of heritage signi昀椀cance including war memorials and avenues of honour.

            3. Protect trees with heritage signi昀椀cance.

            Housing
            Housing within the Shire is currently dominated by detached dwellings in both urban and rural
            areas. The urban area includes the Urban Established Area and the Urban Growth Area, while the
            rural area comprises Townships and rural-residential development.

            The urban area in the Shire will continue to attract predominantly young families into the foreseeable
            future. However, as the housing market progressively matures and the needs of households change
            there will be increasing demand for more diverse forms of housing.

            Accommodation for older people in townships is important, particularly where the unavailability
            of such accommodation would lead to people being forced to leave a community with which they
            have a strong association.

            The indiscriminate development of land for small lot rural and rural residential purposes may result
            in extensive land and water degradation, loss of high quality agricultural land and unnecessarily
            high development and maintenance costs. This type of development requires careful management,
            including:

               Rural residential development, de昀椀ned as single dwellings on lots of between 0.4 hectare and
               2.0 hectares.

               Rural living, de昀椀ned as residential development on lots between 2 hectares and 16 hectares.

            Council’s strategic directions for housing are to:

            1. Provide for diversity of housing types and densities, including increased housing density around
               activity centres.

            2. Provide opportunities for development of ‘affordable housing’.

            3. Integrate rural residential and rural living developments with an urban area or township.

            4. Facilitate diversity of housing choices in rural townships while ensuring consistency with the
               character of the township.

            5. Minimise the impacts of rural residential and rural living developments on the environmental
               characteristics and constraints of the area.

            6. Minimise the encroachment of rural residential and rural living developments on agricultural
               land.

            Economic development
            Local employment for the growing resident population is largely serviced by activity centres and
            the ‘Of昀椀cer-Pakenham State-Signi昀椀cant Industrial Precinct’ identi昀椀ed in Plan Melbourne 2017-2050
            (2017). There is currently a high level of commuting by residents to areas outside the municipality
            for employment. The employment corridor comprises approximately 2,500 hectares to the south
            of the Princes Freeway. When fully developed, this employment corridor will be a major business
            and employment provider for residents of the Shire and Melbourne’s south-east region.

            Page 12 of 1548
02.03-8                                            CARDINIA PLANNING SCHEME

13/03/2026  Smaller industrial precincts are located in Emerald, Maryknoll, Beacons昀椀eld, Of昀椀cer, Bunyip,
C271card    Koo Wee Rup and Lang Lang. A number of existing industries add value to the process of
            agricultural production.

            The South East Industrial Business Park located at the intersection of Bald Hill Road and Koo
            Wee Rup Road, Pakenham, provides 167 hectares of industrial land.

            Tourism also plays an important role within the wider business community, with opportunities for
            visitors to experience the area’s boutique farm produce, arts and crafts, cultural and historic
            locations, and the natural environment.

            The Cardinia Western Port Green Wedge also has scope to build a successful tourism industry
            based on its produce. There needs to be a balanced approach between supporting new and growing
            businesses and protecting the green wedge environment and rural assets upon which the business
            is based.

            Council’s strategic directions for economic development are to:

            1. Develop diverse local employment opportunities to meet the needs of a growing residential
               population.

            2. Maintain agriculture as a strong and sustainable economic activity within the municipality.

            3. Direct commercial activities along arterial roads to within strategic nodes.

            4. Encourage the establishment of tourism land uses in rural townships.

            5. Support the development of the State-signi昀椀cant Pakenham-Of昀椀cer Industrial Precinct as a
               major provider of employment for south-east Melbourne.

            6. Support tourist attractions of regional or State signi昀椀cance including:

                   The Pakenham Racecourse and associated facilities.

                   The Puf昀椀ng Billy Tourist Railway and associated facilities.

                   Gumbuya World.

            7. Provide additional industrial land to the south of the Koo Wee Rup town centre to facilitate the
               development of an additional industry and service industry precinct within the township and
               encourage local employment opportunities.

            Transport
            Pedestrian and cycling paths are important to support active lifestyles.

            The sparse nature of settlement in the municipality affects the viability of providing public transport
            to all residents. The limited public transport services currently available is an issue of concern
            raised consistently by the community.

            The Princes Highway and the Princes Freeway corridor runs east-west through the centre of the
            Shire and provides a demarcation between the hills in the north and the alluvial plains to the south.
            The corridor is a key road and rail link between Melbourne, the Latrobe Valley and Gippsland.
            The South Gippsland Highway is a key link to South Gippsland and a tourist route to Phillip Island.

            The freeways and highways that cross the Shire pass through both urban and rural areas and carry
            a large volume of traf昀椀c, including freight and tourist traf昀椀c. Development along these arterial
            roads needs to be carefully managed to ensure that the ef昀椀cient and safe movement of traf昀椀c and
            visual amenity is maintained and enhanced.

            Future development in the Urban Growth Area will increase the demand for local roads
            infrastructure. There is also a present need to provide adequate roads and streets in the townships
            and to upgrade the existing local road network to support economic development and maintain
            environmental values.

13/03/2026  With continuous major population growth, Cardinia Shire and surrounding areas would bene昀椀t
C271card    from improved tourism and trade connections from the development of a new airport. The
            employment bene昀椀t to the region would also be signi昀椀cant.

            Council has identi昀椀ed potential locations for a third airport between Koo Wee Rup and Lang Lang.

            Council’s strategic directions for transport are to:

            1. Support and provide for the establishment of the Great Southern Rail Trail.

            2. Support the creation of a regional open space network along Cardinia Creek and a multi-use
               trail linking the network to the Upper Beacons昀椀eld township.

            3. Facilitate the completion of the Lang Lang bypass to keep the heavy vehicles associated with
               the sand extraction industry out of the Town Centre.

            4. Support the upgrading of both the Pakenham and Of昀椀cer railway stations as a key element of
               these major activity centres.

            5. Support new railway stations and upgrades of existing railway stations.

            6. Provide east-west connections within the southern parts of the urban growth area.

            7. Provide for the extension at Thompsons Road from Cranbourne through to Koo Wee Rup
               Road.

            8. Provide for the extension of Grices Road from Berwick South to Cardinia Road to an arterial
               road standard.

            9. Encourage the integration of public transport linkages to improve access to higher education
               facilities outside of the municipality including Federation University and Chisholm TAFE.

            10. Provide for greater connectivity and infrastructure that encourages physical activity (including
               walking, cycling and recreational horse riding).

            Infrastructure
            Infrastructure provision is one of the major issues facing the Cardinia Shire over the coming
            decades. The timely provision of physical and social infrastructure is necessary to foster economic
            development, ensure the wellbeing of the community and protect the environment. The provision
            of local recreational and community facilities assists in bringing people together and developing
            a cohesive community.

            The population in the Shire is primarily focused on the activity centres and townships, with a
            growing emphasis on the urban growth corridor. It is important that all residents have a reasonable
            level of access to a range of services consistent with community needs, including rural townships.

            There is a diversity of age groups within the Shire and it is important to provide services to meet
            the needs of particular age groups such as children, youth and the aged.

            Cardinia Shire has a signi昀椀cant amount of regional open space, including Aura Vale Lake Park at
            Cardinia Reservoir, Gembrook Regional Park, Bunyip State Park and Emerald Lake Park. In
            addition, further regional parklands are proposed along the Cardinia Creek to both protect the
            environmental values of the corridor and provide a regional passive recreation resource, in
            recognition of the projected population growth in the Casey-Cardinia Growth Area.

            There are also other signi昀椀cant waterways and streams throughout the Municipality that provide
            passive open space linkages.

            Council’s strategic directions for infrastructure are to:

            1. Facilitate the delivery of arts and cultural facilities.

            2. Improve provision and access to higher education and skills development for residents and
               support the establishment of a higher education facility within Pakenham.

            3. Develop open space linkages.

5. Provide active, passive and environmental open space, including varied play spaces, within the

02/09/2025  PURPOSES OF THIS PLANNING SCHEME
VC283          To provide a clear and consistent framework within which decisions about the use and
               development of land can be made.
               To express state, regional, local and community expectations for areas and land uses.

            THE PEOPLE’S PANEL VISION FOR VICTORIA

            Victorians in quality housing, transport, employment, environment and connectivity, will require
            input from community, government, local businesses and industry alike.
            We will create a society that caters to the unique needs of all Victorians, nurturing individual health
            through physical and cultural recreation.

02/09/2025  Objective
VC283       To facilitate the sustainable growth and development of Victoria and deliver choice and opportunity
            for all Victorians through a network of settlements.

            Strategies
            Plan for the delivery of 2.24 million homes across Victoria by 2051.
            Develop sustainable communities through a settlement framework that:

               Offers a range of housing choices.
               Provides convenient access to jobs, services, infrastructure and community facilities.
               Takes into account regional and municipal contexts and frameworks.
            Focus investment and growth in:
               Melbourne Central City.
               Metropolitan Activity Centres and Suburban Rail Loop Precincts in Metropolitan Melbourne.
               Priority Precincts (including the Suburban Rail Loop East Precincts).
               Major regional cities of Ballarat, Bendigo and Geelong.
                Regional cities of Horsham, Latrobe City, Mildura, Shepparton, Wangaratta, Warrnambool
               and Wodonga.
            Manage the expansion of settlements by:
               Creating and reinforcing settlement boundaries. Where no settlement boundary is identi昀椀ed,
               limit the expansion of a settlement to the extent of existing urban zoned land.
               Promoting and capitalising on opportunities for urban renewal and in昀椀ll redevelopment.
               Limiting urban sprawl and directing growth into existing settlements.
               Ensuring land that may be required for future urban expansion is not compromised.
            Provide for growth in population and development of facilities and services across a regional or
            sub-regional network in accordance with housing targets.
            Plan for development and investment opportunities that make best use of existing and planned
            transport infrastructure.
            Coordinate transport, communications and economic linkages between settlements through the
            identi昀椀cation of servicing priorities.
            Strengthen transport links on national networks for the movement of commodities.
            Deliver networks of high-quality integrated settlements, suburbs and towns that:
               Are great places with a strong identity and sense of place.
               Are inclusive, prosperous, liveable and sustainable.
               Comprise a form and density that supports healthy, active and sustainable transport.
               Are based around compact existing or planned activity centres to maximise accessibility to
               facilities and services.
               Concentrate retail, of昀椀ce-based employment, community facilities and services in central
               locations.
            Facilitate environmentally resilient settlements by:
               Integrating the management of water resources into the urban environment in a way that supports
               water security, public health, environment and amenity outcomes.

11.01-1L-02 Cockatoo

13/03/2026   General Strategies
C271card

             Ensure that use or development within the Cockatoo township is generally consistent with the
             Cockatoo Township Strategy (March 2008), including the Cockatoo Framework Plan (Figure 1).

             Residential development strategies

             Maintain and enhance the ‘rural country’ character of Cockatoo through the retention of larger
             residential lots, the retention of existing remnant vegetation (particular canopy trees) and the use
             of building materials and colours that complement the natural environment.

                                                                           Page 30 of 1548
                                       CARDINIA PLANNING SCHEME

Design development in accordance with the Precinct Character Guidelines in the Cockatoo Township
Strategy (Cardinia Shire Council, March 2008).
Maintain a diverse range of lot sizes within the township.
Encourage permeable fences to enhance the bushland setting.
Avoid residential development where the land has a slope of greater than 20 per cent or is designated
‘very poor’ in the Land Capability Study for the Cardinia Shire, Department of Natural Resources
and the Environment, February 1997.
Economic development strategies
Encourage retail and commercial land use and development to be located in the Cockatoo town
centre.
Support uses that operate during the evening and weekend (such as restaurants and cafes) in
McBride Street.
Facilitate a small service industry within the Cockatoo town centre.
Town centre design strategies
Design developments to meet the preferred height of buildings along McBride Street.
Design second storeys so that they are not visually intrusive, and do not interrupt view lines from
Belgrave-Gembrook Road or Pakenham Road.
Ensure that any development of the vacant land on Fairbridge Lane enhances the visual amenity
of McBride Street.
Discourage the use of roller shutters on shop fronts.
Town centre design policy guidelines
Consider as relevant:

   Providing for up to two storey buildings as the preferred height immediate to McBride Street.

11.01-1L-09 Western Port Green Wedge

13/03/2026  Policy application
C271card

            This policy applies to all land within Cardinia Shire’s portion of the Western Port Green Wedge
            as identi昀椀ed on Cardinia Western Port Green Wedge Precincts Map forming part of this clause.

                                                                             Page 46 of 1548
                                       CARDINIA PLANNING SCHEME

Objective
To ensure that land uses are carefully located and managed to be consistent with the vision for the
Cardinia Western Port Green Wedge.

General strategies
Maintain and protect the highly productive agricultural land from incompatible uses including
non-soil based agricultural uses (e.g. animal husbandry, beef and dairy farming, poultry farming).
Minimise the risk of 昀氀ooding which impacts on agricultural activities in the Koo Wee Rup Flood
Protection District.
Protect the values and assets of the green wedge by preventing further encroachment of urban
development into the Western Port Green Wedge.
Support future extractive indurcty in the area noinated as an Extractive Industry Interest Area
(EIIA) within the Western Port Green Wedge while ensuring a balance between the extraction of
natural resources and the intents of Precicnts 1, 2 and 3.

Precinct 1: Agriculture, horticulture and soil based food production strategies
Encourage non-soil based agricultural uses (e.g. animal husbandry, beef and dairy farming) to the
land surrounding the Special Use Zone – Schedule 1.
Discourage non-rural uses such as primary, secondary schools and places of worship from locating
within the precinct (particularly in the SUZ1) and locate these types of uses within the existing
townships and within the green wedge land that adjoins the urban growth boundary, subject to
strategic justi昀椀cation.
Support and protect the existing vegetable industry, in particular the asparagus growing region.
Encourage lot consolidation through the entire precinct to increase the economic viability of
agricultural land.
Support subsidiary visitor related activity, including farm gate sales of crops and goods produced
in situ, cellar door sales and ancillary farm stay accommodation.

Precinct 2: Coastal strategies
Enhance and encourage agriculture on land situated outside environmentally sensitive coastal areas
and outside of land containing coastal acid sulphate soils.
Discourage non-rural uses such as primary, secondary schools and places of worship.

Precinct 3: Railway strategies
Discourage non-rural uses such as primary, secondary schools and places of worship from locating
within the precinct and locate these types of uses within the existing townships and within the
green wedge land that adjoins the urban growth boundary, subject to strategic justi昀椀cation.
Encourage non-soil based agricultural uses (e.g. animal husbandry, beef and dairy farming).
Encourage and support the use of agriculture and the provision of biodiversity to ensure that land
use is compatible with the adjacent Precinct 1.

Policy document
Consider as relevant:

   Cardinia Western Port Green Wedge Management Plan (Cardinia Shire Council, May 2017).

            of (non-freight) trips in highly accessible activity centres.

            Improve access by walking, cycling and public transport to services and facilities.

            Support the continued growth and diversi昀椀cation of activity centres to give communities access

02/09/2025  Objective
VC283       To plan for sustainable coastal development.

            Strategies
            Plan and manage coastal population growth and increased visitation so that impacts do not cause
            unsustainable use of coastal resources.
            Support a network of diverse coastal settlements that provide for a broad range of housing types,
            economic opportunities and services.
            Minimise linear urban sprawl along the coastal edge and ribbon development in rural landscapes.
            Protect areas between settlements for non-urban use.
            Limit development in identi昀椀ed coastal hazard areas, on ridgelines, primary coastal dune systems,
            shorelines of estuaries, wetlands and low-lying coastal areas, or where coastal processes may be
            detrimentally impacted.
            Encourage the restructure of old and inappropriate subdivisions to reduce development impacts
            on the environment.
            Ensure a sustainable water supply, stormwater management and sewerage treatment for all
            development.
            Minimise the quantity and enhance the quality of stormwater discharge from new development

            Prevent the development of new residential canal estates.

10/06/2022  ENVIRONMENTAL AND LANDSCAPE VALUES
VC216
            Planning should help to protect the health of ecological systems and the biodiversity they support
            (including ecosystems, habitats, species and genetic diversity) and conserve areas with identi昀椀ed
            environmental and landscape values.

            Planning must implement environmental principles for ecologically sustainable development that
            have been established by international and national agreements. Foremost amongst the national
            agreements is the Intergovernmental Agreement on the Environment, which sets out key principles
            for environmental policy in Australia. Other agreements include the National Strategy for
            Ecologically Sustainable Development, National Greenhouse Strategy, the National Water Quality
            Management Strategy, Australia's Strategy for Nature 2019-2030, the National Forest Policy
            Statement and National Environment Protection Measures.

            Planning should protect, restore and enhance sites and features of nature conservation, biodiversity,
            geological or landscape value.

12.01-1S    Protection of biodiversity

30/10/2025  Objective
VC291       To protect and enhance Victoria’s biodiversity.

            Strategies
            Use biodiversity information to identify important areas of biodiversity, including key habitat for
            rare or threatened species and communities, and strategically valuable biodiversity sites.

            Strategically plan for the protection and conservation of Victoria’s important areas of biodiversity.

            Ensure that decision making takes into account the impacts of land use and development on
            Victoria’s biodiversity, including consideration of:

               Cumulative impacts.

               Fragmentation of habitat.

               The spread of pest plants, animals and pathogens into natural ecosystems.

            Avoid impacts of land use and development on important areas of biodiversity.

            Consider impacts of any change in land use or development that may affect the biodiversity value
            of national parks and conservation reserves or nationally and internationally signi昀椀cant sites;
            including wetlands and wetland wildlife habitat designated under the Convention on Wetlands of
            International Importance (the Ramsar Convention) and sites utilised by species listed under the
            Japan-Australia Migratory Birds Agreement (JAMBA), the China-Australia Migratory Birds
            Agreement (CAMBA), or the Republic of Korea-Australia Migratory Bird Agreement
            (ROKAMBA).

            Assist in the identi昀椀cation, protection and management of important areas of biodiversity.

            Assist in the establishment, protection and re-establishment of links between important areas of
            biodiversity, including through a network of green spaces and large-scale native vegetation corridor
            projects.

            Support land use and development that contributes to protecting and enhancing habitat for
            indigenous plants and animals in urban areas.

            Policy guidelines
            Consider as relevant:

               State biodiversity information maintained by the Department of Energy, Environment and
               Climate Action.

            Policy documents

            Native vegetation management

            Objective
            To ensure that there is no net loss to biodiversity as a result of the removal, destruction or lopping
            of native vegetation.

            Strategies
            Ensure decisions that involve, or will lead to, the removal, destruction or lopping of native
            vegetation, apply the three-step approach in accordance with the Guidelines for the removal,
            destruction or lopping of native vegetation (Department of Energy, Environment and Climate
            Action, 2025):

               Avoid the removal, destruction or lopping of native vegetation.

               Minimise impacts from the removal, destruction or lopping of native vegetation that cannot be
               avoided.

               Provide an offset to compensate for the biodiversity impact from the removal, destruction or
               lopping of native vegetation.

12.03-1S    River and riparian corridors, waterways, lakes, wetlands and billabongs

20/01/2026  Policy Application
VC278       This policy applies to land in proximity to a waterway, including all land within 200 metres from
            the centreline of a waterway.

            Objective
            To protect and enhance waterway systems including river and riparian corridors, waterways, lakes,
            wetlands and billabongs.

            Strategies
            Protect the environmental, cultural and landscape values of all waterway systems as signi昀椀cant
            economic, environmental and cultural assets.

            Conserve waterway systems and the landscapes and environmental values surrounding them by:

               Protecting ecological values, indigenous vegetation, terrestrial and aquatic habitats.

               Encouraging biodiversity.

               Recognising that waterways are a connected system from source to mouth, including tributaries,
               con昀氀uences, wetlands and billabongs creating a living entity.

            Ensure waterway corridors are of adequate width to allow for the natural systems and functions
            of the environment and landscape to occur while incorporating potential impacts from climate
            change.

            Sensitively design and site development to maintain and enhance the waterway system and the
            surrounding landscape setting, environmental assets, and ecological and hydrological systems.

            Address the impacts of use and development on drought and 昀氀ooding events at a catchment and
            site scale to protect the health and natural function of waterway systems and their surrounding
            landscape and environment.

            Protect geomorphology, bank stability and 昀氀ood management capacity to strengthen the
            environmental value and health of waterway systems by:

               Retaining, enhancing and re-establishing indigenous riparian vegetation along waterway systems,
               ensuring it responds to the bush昀椀re hazard of a location.

               Enhancing and re-establishing both terrestrial and aquatic habitats and their linkages along and
               surrounding waterway systems.

               Limiting earthworks in proximity to waterway systems to minimise alterations to
               geomorphology, natural drainage, natural 昀氀ows, volumes and water quality.

               Facilitating the restoration of waterway systems through the removal of weeds, invasive species
               and pests.

            Enhance a sense of place and landscape identity by:

               Conserving areas of identi昀椀ed Victorian Aboriginal cultural heritage signi昀椀cance relating to
               waterway systems.

               Retaining and re-establishing vegetation, including grasslands and canopy trees, surrounding
               waterway systems to enhance and connect to the landscape setting, ensuring it responds to the
               bush昀椀re hazard of a location.

               Protecting existing topographic features and maintaining a sense of naturalness through sensitive
               design and siting.

               Recognising the cultural values, aesthetic qualities and identity of waterway systems.

            Retain and enhance the recreation and amenity values along waterway systems by:

                                      Page 74 of 1548
                                       CARDINIA PLANNING SCHEME

   Planning for surrounding green spaces as recreation and tourism resources without adversely
   impacting environmental values and 昀氀ood management capacity.
   Protecting and enhancing parklands for their economic, social and environmental values.
   Protecting and enhancing public access to waterway systems and surrounding parklands.
   Enhancing existing and providing new green links, pedestrian and cycle connections and open
   space.
   Discouraging privatisation of spaces that interface with or provide access to waterway systems.
   Avoiding overshadowing of waterway systems, their banks and adjacent public open space.
   Promoting safety by maximising visibility and passive surveillance and providing good
   connections and access.
Design and site development to maintain and enhance the natural environment of waterway systems
by:
   Minimising the visual intrusion of development on the natural landscape views from major
   roads, bridge crossings, public open space, recreation trails and within waterway systems
   themselves.
   Ensuring development is visually subordinate to the local landscape setting, including through
   the use of vegetation to 昀椀lter views of development and avoiding overshadowing.
   Ensuring development adjacent to waterways adopts high quality materials and respectful
   design and siting.
   Avoiding impeding the natural 昀氀ow of waterways and future 昀氀ood events.
   Directing growth to established settlements where water and wastewater can be managed.

Policy guidelines
Consider as relevant:

   Locating earthworks, including dams, a minimum of 50 metres from waterway systems.
   Locating development a minimum of 50 metres from the banks of waterway systems.
   The Aboriginal cultural heritage sensitivity and impacts of development within a 200 metre
   distance from the centreline of a waterway system.
   The views of 昀氀oodplain and waterway managers.
   Any regional catchment strategy and related plans approved under the Catchment and Land
   Protection Act 1994.

            昀氀ora and fauna and sensitive landscapes.

            Ensure that there is a mixture of use and development to cater for users of alpine areas in all
            seasons.

            Recognise the distinct environments, infrastructure needs and capabilities to support different
            activities of each alpine resort and other alpine areas.

            Provide for the development of consolidated alpine villages, including a diverse range of
            employment, social and economic opportunities.

            Promote development for active recreation solely at Falls Creek, Lake Mountain, Mt Buffalo, Mt
            Baw Baw, Mt Buller and Mt Hotham.

            Promote intensive residential and commercial development at Falls Creek, Mt Baw Baw, Mt Buller
            and Mt Hotham.

            Maintain Mt Stirling as an all-season nature based tourist, recreational and educational resource.

            Ensure that the sustainable long term planning and management of Victoria’s six alpine resorts is
            consistent with the strategic directions contained in the Alpine Resorts Strategic Plan 2020-2025
            Responding to a Changing Climate (Victorian Government, Alpine Resorts Co-ordinating Council,
            2019).

            Develop, monitor and regularly review the Alpine Resort Environmental Management Plans and
            Comprehensive Development Plans for each alpine resort, recognising their unique characteristics,
            constraints and opportunities.

            Encourage best practice in design that responds to the alpine character of the area.

            Ensure heritage places are protected and conserved, including Aboriginal cultural heritage and
            post contact heritage places.

            Ensure that increases in skier, pedestrian and vehicular activity in the resorts do not compromise
            public safety or the accessibility and capacity of ski 昀椀elds, services, commercial activity and
            development of trailheads.

            Implement approved plans, manage development and work with Alpine Resort Management Boards
            to effectively operate alpine resorts and protect alpine resources.

            Ensure that the use and development of land responds to potential environmental risks and
            contributes to maintaining or improving the environmental quality of alpine environments.

13.01-2S    Coastal inundation and erosion

05/09/2025  Objective
VC268       To plan for and manage coastal hazard risk and climate change impacts.

            Strategies
            Plan for sea level rise of not less than 0.8 metres by 2100 and allow for the combined effects of
            tides, storm surges, coastal processes and local conditions such as topography and geology when
            assessing risks and coastal impacts associated with climate change.
            Ensure that land subject to hazards is identi昀椀ed and appropriately managed to ensure that future
            use and development is not at risk.
            Avoid use and development in areas vulnerable to coastal inundation and erosion.
            Respond to marine and coastal processes in the context of the coastal compartment type.
            Assess the effectiveness, costs, bene昀椀ts, impacts (direct, cumulative and synergistic) and path
            dependency of available adaptation options in the following order:
            1. non-intervention
            2. avoid
            3. nature-based methods
            4. accommodate
            5. retreat
            6. protect
            Ensure that development or protective works that seek to respond to coastal hazard risks avoid
            detrimental impacts on coastal processes.

13.02-1S    Bushfire planning

16/06/2026  Policy application
VC312       This policy must be applied to all planning and decision making under the Act relating to land:

               in a bush昀椀re prone area;

               in a Bush昀椀re Management Overlay; or

               proposed to be used or developed in a way that may create a bush昀椀re hazard.

            Objective
            To strengthen the resilience of settlements and communities to bush昀椀re through risk-based planning
            that prioritises the protection of human life.

            Strategies
            Give priority to the protection of human life by:

               Prioritising the protection of human life over all other policy considerations.

               Directing population growth and development to low risk locations and ensuring the availability
               of, and reliable access to, areas where human life can be better protected from the effects of
               bush昀椀re.

               Reducing the vulnerability of communities to bush昀椀re through the consideration of bush昀椀re
               risk in decision making at all stages of the planning process.

            Identify bush昀椀re hazard and undertake appropriate risk assessment by:

               Applying the best available science to identify vegetation, topographic and climatic conditions
               that create a bush昀椀re hazard.

               Considering the best available information about bush昀椀re hazard, including the bush昀椀re prone
               area map.

               Applying the Bush昀椀re Management Overlay to land where the extent of vegetation can create
               an extreme bush昀椀re hazard.

               Considering and assessing the bush昀椀re hazard on the basis of:

               – Landscape conditions - meaning conditions in the landscape within 20 kilometres (and
                   potentially up to 75 kilometres) of the site.

               – Local and neighbourhood conditions - meaning conditions in the area within approximately
                   5 kilometres of the site.

               – The site and conditions within 150 metres.

               Consulting with emergency management agencies and the relevant 昀椀re authority early in the
               process to receive their recommendations and implement appropriate bush昀椀re protection
               measures.

               Ensuring that strategic planning documents, planning scheme amendments, planning permit
               applications and development plan approvals properly assess bush昀椀re risk and include
               appropriate bush昀椀re protection measures.

               Not approving development where a landowner or proponent has not satisfactorily demonstrated
               that the relevant policies have been addressed, performance measures satis昀椀ed or bush昀椀re
               protection measures can be adequately implemented.

            Plan to strengthen the resilience of settlements and communities through settlement growth, land
            use and development that prioritises the protection of human life by:

                                      Page 89 of 1548
                                       CARDINIA PLANNING SCHEME

   Assessing the bush昀椀re hazard at different spatial scales (landscape, local and neighbourhood
   and site), the likely 昀椀re behaviour, bush昀椀re risk and the potential for local and
   neighbourhood-scale destruction.

   Directing population growth and development to low-risk locations, being those where:

   – The risk from large bush昀椀res in the wider landscape can be managed including the risk
       associated with higher levels of ember attack.

   – On completion, development will not be exposed to high levels of radiant heat, which is no
       more than 12.5 kilowatts/square metre for locations subject to strategic planning or the
       preparation of a planning scheme amendment.

   – There is reliable access to areas of land where human life can be better protected from the
       effects of bush昀椀re.

   – Bush昀椀re protection measures can be provided to manage the on-going risk from bush昀椀re.

   Ensuring alternative low-risk locations for settlement growth on a regional, municipal, settlement,
   local and neighbourhood basis have been assessed to ensure the proposed location for growth
   prioritises human life.

   Ensuring the bush昀椀re risk to existing and future residents, property and community infrastructure
   will not increase as a result of future land use and development.

   Achieving no net increase in risk to existing and future residents, property and community
   infrastructure, through the implementation of bush昀椀re protection measures and where possible
   reducing bush昀椀re risk overall.

   Not preparing, adopting or approving a plan that will result in the introduction or intensi昀椀cation
   of development in an area that has, or will have on completion, a radiant heat exposure of more
   than 12.5 kilowatts/square metre in the event of a bush昀椀re. In this strategy, 'plan' means a
   strategic plan, policy statement, and amendment to a planning scheme, including an amendment
   to the Planning Policy Framework, or a plan approved under a provision of the planning scheme.
Ensure settlement growth and development approvals can implement bush昀椀re protection measures
without unacceptable biodiversity impacts by discouraging settlement growth and development
in bush昀椀re affected areas that are important areas of biodiversity.
When assessing a planning permit application for a use or development that will result in people
congregating in large numbers:

   consider the risk of bush昀椀re to people, property and community infrastructure;

   require the implementation of appropriate bush昀椀re protection measures to address the identi昀椀ed
   bush昀椀re risk; and

   ensure development can implement bush昀椀re protection measures without unacceptable
   biodiversity impacts.

Policy guidelines
Consider as relevant:

   Any applicable approved state, regional and municipal 昀椀re prevention plan.

Policy documents
Consider as relevant:

   AS 3959-2018 Construction of buildings in bush昀椀re-prone areas (Standards Australia, 2018)

   Design guidelines for settlement planning at the bush昀椀re interface (Department of Environment,
   Land, Water and Planning, 2020)

   The bush昀椀re prone area map.

13.03-1S    Flood planning

20/10/2026  Objective
VC317
            To strengthen the resilience of settlements and communities to 昀氀ood (riverine, coastal and overland
            昀氀ows from stormwater) through risk-based planning that prioritises the protection of human life.

            To assist the protection of:

               Property and community infrastructure from 昀氀ood hazard.

               The natural 昀氀ood carrying capacity of rivers, streams and 昀氀oodways.

               The 昀氀ood storage function of 昀氀oodplains and waterways.

               Floodplain areas of environmental signi昀椀cance or of importance to river, wetland or marine
               and coastal ecosystems and habitats.

            Strategies

            Prioritise the protection of human life over all other policy considerations in areas of high, very
            high and extreme 昀氀ood risk.

            Identify land at moderate, high, very high and extreme 昀氀ood risk within the 1 per cent Annual
            Exceedance Probability (1 in 100 year) 昀氀ood extent or as determined by the 昀氀oodplain management
            authority in planning schemes.

            Apply the Flood Management Zone to land subject to extreme 昀氀ood risk and the Flood Management
            Overlay schedules to land subject to moderate, high and very high 昀氀ood risk.

            Plan for use and development using a rainfall intensity consistent with a high emissions climate
            change scenario, being no less than Shared Socio-economic Pathway SSP3-7.0 median or equivalent,
            to at least the year 2100, where there is a potential risk to human life.

            Plan for 昀氀ood and drainage infrastructure to manage 昀氀ood risk, having regard to asset lifecycles,
            development staging and the need to adapt to climate change, to minimise risk to human life and
            support infrastructure resilience.

            Direct vulnerable use and development away from land that is identi昀椀ed as high, very high and
            extreme 昀氀ood risk.

            Avoid intensifying the impact of 昀氀ooding through inappropriately located use and development.

            Plan for the cumulative impacts of use and development on 昀氀ood behaviour.

            Ensure that development, access and built form design are resilient to the impacts of 昀氀ood and
            future climate conditions.

            Avoid locating community facilities that accommodate vulnerable people (including residential
            aged care facilities, retirement villages, community shelters, child care centres and schools) within
            the 1 per cent Annual Exceedance Probability (1 in 100 year) 昀氀ood extent unless 昀氀ood risk can
            be safely managed through appropriate siting, access and design.

            Avoid locating emergency services and essential infrastructure (including ambulance, police and
            昀椀re stations and hospitals) within the 1 per cent Annual Exceedance Probability (1 in 100 year) 昀氀ood
            extent and where practicable, above the Probable Maximum Flood level, and where this is not
            practicable, ensure they are sited in areas of relatively low 昀氀ood risk and are designed to minimise
            risk and maintain safe access and operational continuity during and after 昀氀oods.

            Locate use and development involving the storage or disposal of environmentally hazardous
            industrial and agricultural chemicals or wastes and other dangerous goods (including intensive
            animal industries and sewage treatment plants) outside the Probable Maximum Flood level unless
            site design and management:

               Prevents contact between such substances and 昀氀oodwaters.

               Preserves or improves the 昀氀ood carrying capacity and 昀氀ood storage functions of the 昀氀oodplain.

                                      Page 93 of 1548

Ensure land use minimises the risk of waterway contamination occurring during 昀氀oods.
Ensure 昀氀oodplains can function as temporary storage to moderate peak 昀氀ows and minimise
downstream impacts.

            and productivity.

            Avoid permanent removal of productive agricultural land from the state's agricultural base without
            consideration of the economic importance of the land for the agricultural production and processing
            sectors.

            Protect productive farmland that is of strategic signi昀椀cance in the local or regional context.

            Protect productive agricultural land from unplanned loss due to permanent changes in land use.

            Prevent inappropriately dispersed urban activities in rural areas.

            Protect strategically important agricultural and primary production land from incompatible uses.

            Limit new housing development in rural areas by:

               Directing housing growth into existing settlements.

               Discouraging development of isolated small lots in the rural zones from use for dwellings or
               other incompatible uses.

               Encouraging consolidation of existing isolated small lots in rural zones.

            Identify areas of productive agricultural land by consulting with the Department of Energy,
            Environment and Climate Action and using available information.

            In considering a proposal to use, subdivide or develop agricultural land, consider the:

               Desirability and impacts of removing the land from primary production, given its agricultural
               productivity.

               Impacts on the continuation of primary production on adjacent land, with particular regard to
               land values and the viability of infrastructure for such production.

               Compatibility between the proposed or likely development and the existing use of the
               surrounding land.

               The potential impacts of land use and development on the spread of plant and animal pests
               from areas of known infestation into agricultural areas.

               Land capability.

            Avoid the subdivision of productive agricultural land from diminishing the long-term productive
            capacity of the land.

            Give priority to the re-structure of inappropriate subdivisions where they exist on productive
            agricultural land.

            Balance the potential off-site effects of a use or development proposal (such as degradation of soil
            or water quality and land salinisation) against the bene昀椀ts of the proposal.

            of life consistent with accepted standards not be diminished due to the impacts of extractive

            To facilitate signs that allow for the reasonable identi昀椀cation and marketing of businesses in
            Cardinia while enhancing the character of a building, site and area.

Strategies

General
Encourage signs that are integrated with architectural features and compliment the style and
character of the host building, abutting buildings and the overall landscape or streetscape and avoid
signs that:

   Obscure a building’s architectural form, features or glazed surfaces.
   Protrude above roo昀氀ines or parapets, or beyond the edges of fascia or walls of the host building.
Ensure that signs for individual businesses in joint occupancy buildings are of a uniform size,
shape and presentation.
Enable signs that identify the business and service provided on the site and avoid signs that promote
other businesses or details of product/s sold.
Ensure signs sensitively respond to the character of the building, site and area by minimising and
consolidating signage to avoid visual clutter.
Ensure that signs are not located on the road or rail reserve.
Design signs to integrate with heritage buildings or objects to ensure the buildings and architectural
features and detailing are not obscured.
Use materials and lighting to achieve energy ef昀椀ciency.
Conceal electrical services to a sign.
Design and locate signs in a manner that accounts for the long-term maintenance needs and the
ease of changing messages.
Provide adequate space for all occupancies to display signage where a building or site is occupied
by more than one business.
Ensure signs do not compromise the structural integrity and safety of the host building/structure.
Design signs to be clearly legible in order to support safe pedestrian, cyclist and road movements,
using:
   Materials and colours that have suf昀椀cient contrast between the text and background.
   Letters/symbols that are readable both during the day as well as the night.
   Measures to eliminate glare.
Ensure signs do not impair the effectiveness of surrounding security and emergency signs.
Ensure signs do not affect road or rail safety through glare and re昀氀ection or the obscuring of
sightlines.
Discourage internally illuminated, 昀氀oodlit, animated, electronic and re昀氀ective signs on sites or in
locations where they will impact upon residential amenity.
Design signs to enhance major entrances and gateways to the municipality.
Protect areas of environmental and natural signi昀椀cance by limiting signage within, adjoining or
facing these areas.

Policy guidelines
Consider as relevant:

   Locating signs at a safe clearance above the footpath (a minimum of 2700mm from ground
   level) and are set back at least 750mm from the kerb line if the signs are located on street
   fronting development and protrude from the property boundary.
   Providing for direction signs that are:

   – Limited to one per road entry point.
   – Less than 0.3 square metres in size.

   That signage has an integrated and co-ordinated sign package in terms of colour, graphics and
   placement.

Commercial (shop and office) signs

Strategies
Signs located in commercial (shop and of昀椀ce) areas should stimulate interest in the business or
service provided on the site and enhance the vitality and visual amenity of the commercial area.
Design signs on freestanding land used for commercial purposes, including service station, retail
premises, freeway service centre, of昀椀ce (medical centre) and veterinary centre land uses to be
incorporated into the building form and contribute to good urban design outcomes.
Avoid views from windows being obscured to maintain passive surveillance of pedestrian activity
areas, car parking areas and streets.

Policy Guidelines
Consider as relevant:

   Limiting signs painted in corporate colours on the exterior of a building with a direct frontage
   to a road or car parking area to the front façade.

Commercial (shop and office) areas
   Avoiding above verandah signs, sky signs, high wall signs and bunting signs.
   Limiting signs to no more than 50 per cent of the wall area above a verandah, or if no verandah
   30 per cent of the total front facade wall.
   Limiting signs to no more than 75 per cent of an awning fascias.

Freestanding 'Pad' sites
   Limiting business identi昀椀cation signs to signs that are:
   – Consistent in size and form, where there is more than one sign.
   – Located on the awning fascia, verandah fascia or parapet.

   Providing for pole and free-standing panel signs that are:
   – Limited to one sign per road frontage.
   – Less than seven (7) metres in height.
   – Incorporated into the landscaping treatment.

15.01-3S    Subdivision design

01/01/2024  Objective
VC250       To ensure the design of subdivisions achieves attractive, safe, accessible, diverse and sustainable
            neighbourhoods.

            Strategies
            In the development of new residential areas and in the redevelopment of existing areas, subdivision
            should be designed to create liveable and sustainable communities by:

               Creating compact neighbourhoods that have walkable distances between activities.
               Developing activity centres in appropriate locations with a mix of uses and services and access
               to public transport.
               Creating neighbourhood centres that include services to meet day to day needs.
               Creating urban places with a strong sense of place that are functional, safe and attractive.
               Providing a range of lot sizes to suit a variety of dwelling and household types to meet the
               needs and aspirations of different groups of people.
               Creating landscaped streets and a network of open spaces to meet a variety of needs with links
               to regional parks where possible.
               Protecting and enhancing habitat for native 昀氀ora and fauna, and providing opportunities for
               people to experience nature in urban areas.
               Facilitating an urban structure where neighbourhoods are clustered to support larger activity
               centres served by high quality public transport.
               Reduce car dependency by allowing for:
               – Convenient and safe public transport.

               – Safe and attractive spaces and networks for walking and cycling.

               – Subdivision layouts that allow easy movement within and between neighbourhoods.

               – A convenient and safe road network.

               Minimising exposure of sensitive uses to air and noise pollution from the transport system.
               Being accessible to people with disabilities.
               Creating an urban structure that:
               – Responds to climate related hazards.

               – Incorporates integrated water management, including sustainable irrigation of open space.

               – Minimises peak demand on the electricity network.

               – Supports energy ef昀椀ciency and solar energy generation through urban layout and lot
                   orientation.

               – Supports waste minimisation and increased resource recovery.

               Providing utilities and services that support the uptake of renewable energy technologies, such
               as microgrids and energy storage systems, including batteries.
               Providing all-electric lots.

               Can be supplied with electricity, water and good quality road access.

18.01-1S    Land use and transport integration

04/02/2026  Objective
VC265       To facilitate access to social, cultural and economic opportunities by effectively integrating land
            use and transport.

            Strategies
            Plan and develop a transport system that facilitates:

               Social and economic inclusion for all people and builds community wellbeing.

               The best use of existing social and economic infrastructure.

               A reduction in the distances people have to travel to access jobs and services.

               Better access to, and greater mobility within, local communities.

               Network-wide ef昀椀ciency and coordinated operation.
            Plan land use and development to:

               Protect existing transport infrastructure from encroachment or detriment that would impact on
               the current or future function of the asset.

               Protect transport infrastructure that is in delivery from encroachment or detriment that would
               impact on the construction or future function of the asset.

               Protect planned transport infrastructure from encroachment or detriment that would impact
               deliverability or future operation.

               Protect identi昀椀ed potential transport infrastructure from being precluded by land use and
               development.
